The Blue-spotted flathead, Platycephalus caeruleopunctatus, is an ambush predator inhabiting sandy substrates along the eastern Australian coastline. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum total length of approximately 45 centimeters [Li = approximately 45 centimeters], representing the upper limit of its somatic growth trajectory. In coastal embayments and estuarine zones, larger individuals are typically encountered in deeper channels where they exploit ample prey resources. A length-weight relationship derived from local specimens suggests that the largest adults achieve an ultimate wet body mass of around 1704 grams [Wwi = around 1704 grams], a value consistent with the robust, dorsoventrally flattened body plan characteristic of platycephalids. This substantial mass is supported by a diet of small demersal fishes and crustaceans, which the flathead captures through a rapid lunge from its buried position. Growth rates appear to be moderated by seasonal water temperatures and prey availability, with slower increments during winter months. The observed length distribution in trawl samples shows a sharp decline beyond 40 centimeters, perhaps indicating increased natural mortality among the oldest age classes.

Reproductive development in Platycephalus caeruleopunctatus is closely tied to body size, with individuals reaching the onset of gonadal maturation at a total length of about 22 centimeters [Lp = about 22 centimeters]. This length at puberty marks the transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive investment. Histological examination of gonadal tissue reveals that males typically mature slightly earlier than females, although both sexes exhibit synchronous vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis within the spawning season. The acquisition of mature gonads is energetically demanding, and the species appears to channel a considerable portion of assimilated energy into gamete production once the 22-centimeter benchmark is surpassed. Comparative data from congeners such as Platycephalus conatus indicate a similar pubertal length relative to ultimate size, suggesting a conserved life-history pattern within the genus. Individuals below this threshold allocate resources almost exclusively to length and weight gain, a strategy that maximizes future fecundity.

At a controlled water temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C], experimental rearing trials have yielded key early-life parameters for this species. The incubation period from spawning to yolk-sac larva emergence lasts approximately 7.5 days [ab = approximately 7.5 days], a duration that reflects the rapid embryogenesis typical of warm-water platycephalids at a temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C]. The newly hatched prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. These emerging larvae possess a negligible wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000065 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000065 grams], a value derived from an estimated egg diameter of 0.5 millimeters. This minuscule initial mass highlights the extreme vulnerability of the early larval stages to starvation, predation, and advection away from suitable nursery habitats. The yolk sac is resorbed within two to three days post-hatching, after which successful first feeding on small copepod nauplii becomes critical for continued survival. Mortality during this transitional period is presumed to be substantial in the wild.

Continuing observations under the same thermal regime of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C] have provided estimates of the species' maximum reproductive output. Gravid females are capable of producing roughly 4384 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 4384 eggs per day] during peak spawning, a rate that reflects high fecundity compensating for low per-offspring survival in the pelagic environment. Females can release eggs on consecutive days through the breeding season, and this continuous spawning strategy is energetically expensive, likely supported by the ingestion of energy-rich prey. The maximum reproduction rate in terms of daily egg production is therefore substantial, underscoring a life-history strategy oriented toward high batch fecundity rather than large offspring size. The 23.7 °C regime used in these trials corresponds to mean summer sea surface temperatures across the species' core distribution, suggesting that natural spawning coincides with the warmest months when planktonic food resources are most abundant.

Long-term mark-recapture studies and otolith ageing have clarified the longevity of the Blue-spotted flathead, revealing a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under prevailing environmental conditions of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C]. This lifespan is moderate for a teleost of its ultimate size, balancing the high fecundity of short-lived individuals with the cumulative reproductive output of older, larger females. The oldest age classes, typically corresponding to individuals exceeding 40 centimeters in total length, contribute disproportionately to the annual egg production due to their increased body mass and gonadal volume. Age-specific mortality appears to increase after the sixth year, possibly linked to the energetic costs of repeated spawning bouts and the onset of reproductive senescence. The combination of an 8-year lifespan and high daily fecundity yields a lifetime reproductive output that ensures population persistence despite intense predation pressure on eggs and larvae. Understanding this longevity is critical for stock assessment and fisheries management, as overexploitation of older age classes could rapidly deplete the spawning biomass.
